title: Homotopy mapping property of enriched arrow inversion
statement:
Use small simplicial categories, their mapping simplicial sets, and their categories of path components as in [lem-coef-simplicial-interval-lifting]. A Dwyer--Kan equivalence is a simplicial functor inducing weak homotopy equivalences on mapping sets and an equivalence of categories of path components. Give these categories the model structure with these weak equivalences, generating cofibrations $I$ and generating trivial cofibrations $J$ of that node, with acyclicity as in [lem-coef-simplicial-interval-cell-stability]. Write $h\mathrm{sCat}$ for its model homotopy category, computed using cofibrant-fibrant replacements and homotopy classes. Choose universes containing all categories displayed. For a small simplicial category $C$ and a set $W$ of vertex arrows, let $L_WC$ be the derived pushout of $C\leftarrow\coprod_W[1]\to\coprod_W\mathbb J$, where $[1]$ is the discrete walking arrow and $\mathbb J$ is the discrete two-object groupoid with exactly one arrow for each ordered pair of objects. Write $q:C\to L_WC$ for the structure map. For every small simplicial category $T$, restriction along $q$ is injective on homotopy classes,
$$q^*:\operatorname{Hom}_{h\mathrm{sCat}}(L_WC,T)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{h\mathrm{sCat}}(C,T),$$
and its image consists precisely of the classes whose induced functor $\pi_0C\to\pi_0T$, taken up to natural isomorphism, sends every $w\in W$ to an isomorphism. This homotopy mapping property characterizes $(L_WC,q)$ up to isomorphism under $C$ in $h\mathrm{sCat}$. Enriched functors carrying a specified set of arrows into another induce maps of these localizations, compatible with composition in $h\mathrm{sCat}$.

source.place: Notation A.3.5.1, Remark A.3.5.2, Lemmas A.3.5.3-A.3.5.4 and Proposition A.3.5.5, printed pp.891-893; simplicial-set invertibility is Example A.3.2.18. Read online 2026-10-17; archival HTT WANTED. No Stacks tag states this homotopical theorem.

proof.text: The item declares the Dwyer--Kan model structure with the displayed generating sets $I$ and $J$; this step checks that these data form a model structure. The interval-lifting node supplies completeness and cocompleteness of $\mathrm{sCat}$, the generators, functorial small-object factorizations as a $K\text{-cell}$ map followed by a $K\text{-inj}$ map for $K=I,J$, the retract description of $K\text{-cof}$, the inclusion $J\subseteq I\text{-cof}$, and the description of $J\text{-inj}$ as local Kan fibrations lifting $\pi_0$-invertible vertices. The interval-cell-stability node supplies two-out-of-three and retract closure for the class $W$ of Dwyer--Kan equivalences and says that every relative $J$-cell map is in $W$; hence $J\text{-cof}\subseteq I\text{-cof}\cap W$. The remaining clauses are checked in the next step.

source.place: Sections 1--3, generating maps (C1),(C2),(A1),(A2), Propositions 2.3, 2.5 and Theorem 1.1 via the Kan recognition theorem (Hovey, Model Categories, Theorem 2.1.19); HTT Appendix A.3.2 for the Bergner model structure

proof.text: Continuing the check of the model structure, lifting against $\varnothing\to\{0\}$ is surjectivity on objects, and lifting against $U(\partial\Delta^n)\to U(\Delta^n)$ with the two objects fixed is the lifting problem of $\partial\Delta^n\to\Delta^n$ in one mapping set. By the boundary characterization of trivial Kan fibrations in the Kan model node (including $n=0$), $I\text{-inj}$ consists of the functors that are surjective on objects and trivial Kan fibrations on every mapping set. Such a $p:A\to B$ is a weak equivalence on mapping sets, and $\pi_0p$ is fully faithful and surjective on objects, so $p\in W$; given $a$ and a $\pi_0$-invertible vertex $e:pa\to b$, choose $a'$ over $b$ and a vertex $d:a\to a'$ over $e$ by surjectivity on vertices, and $d$ is invertible in $\pi_0A$ since $\pi_0p$ is fully faithful, so $p\in J\text{-inj}$. Conversely let $p\in W\cap J\text{-inj}$. Each mapping map is a Kan fibration and a weak equivalence, hence a trivial Kan fibration by the Kan model node. For an object $b$ of $B$, essential surjectivity of $\pi_0p$ gives $a$ and an invertible component $pa\to b$; lifting a representing vertex by the equivalence-lifting clause gives $a'$ with $pa'=b$. Thus $I\text{-inj}=W\cap J\text{-inj}$. If $f\in I\text{-cof}\cap W$, factor $f=pj$ with $j\in J\text{-cell}$ and $p\in J\text{-inj}$; two-out-of-three gives $p\in W$, hence $p\in I\text{-inj}$, and the lift in the square with $f$ on the left, $p$ on the right, $j$ on top and the identity at the bottom exhibits $f$ as a retract of $j$, so $f\in J\text{-cof}$. Therefore $(I\text{-cof},W\cap J\text{-inj})$ and $(J\text{-cof},J\text{-inj})$ with $J\text{-cof}=I\text{-cof}\cap W$ are the two weak factorization systems of a model structure with weak equivalences $W$, and its cofibrant-fibrant replacements and homotopy classes compute the declared $h\mathrm{sCat}$ used in the remaining steps.

source.place: Sections 1--3, generating maps (C1),(C2),(A1),(A2), Propositions 2.3, 2.5 and Theorem 1.1 via the Kan recognition theorem (Hovey, Model Categories, Theorem 2.1.19); HTT Appendix A.3.2 for the Bergner model structure

proof.text: Use the framed function complexes of the derived-pushout mapping node: their $n$-simplices are ordinary enriched functors from the $n$th term of a cosimplicial frame into $RT$. Put $X=\operatorname{Map}^h(C,T)$, $Y=\operatorname{Map}^h(\coprod_W[1],T)$ and $Z=\operatorname{Map}^h(\coprod_W\mathbb J,T)$. Applying the node's pushout comparison gives $\operatorname{Map}^h(L_WC,T)\simeq X\times_Y^h Z$, with $q^*$ corresponding to the projection to $X$. Its explicit natural bijection $\pi_0\operatorname{Map}^h(A,T)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{h\mathrm{sCat}}(A,T)$, for $A=C,L_WC$, identifies the path-component map of this projection with the homotopy-class map in the item.

source.place: Sections 5.2 and 5.4; application of the framed derived-pushout mapping theorem stated in the cited node.

proof.text: The coproduct comparison of the derived-pushout mapping node identifies $Y$ with $\prod_{w\in W}Y_w$ and $Z$ with $\prod_{w\in W}Z_w$, where $Y_w=\operatorname{Map}^h([1],T)$ and $Z_w=\operatorname{Map}^h(\mathbb J,T)$, compatibly with restriction. Use the compatible frame choices supplied by the walking-groupoid node: $Z_w\to Y_w$ factors as a trivial Kan fibration $Z_w\to E_w$ followed by inclusion of the invertible-arrow components. The product $p:\prod_w Z_w\to E:=\prod_wE_w$ is again a trivial Kan fibration: for a lifting problem against any boundary inclusion choose a lift in each coordinate, giving the required product lift. This uses the boundary lifting characterization in the Kan model node, including the boundary of $\Delta^0$. The subcomplex $E\subseteq\prod_wY_w$ is a union of components, since an edge has its two endpoints in the same component in every coordinate. The empty product is a point, so the argument includes $W=\varnothing$.

source.place: Appendix A.3.5, with agent argument from the stronger walking-groupoid function-complex lemma; products of trivial Kan fibrations use componentwise boundary lifting.

proof.text: Let $a:X\to Y=\prod_wY_w$ be restriction and put $X_E=X\times_Y E$. Inclusion of a union of components of a Kan complex is a Kan fibration: a horn whose vertices lie in those components has any filler in the ambient Kan complex, and that filler's vertices remain in the same components. Thus $E\to Y$ and $E_w\to Y_w$ are Kan fibrations. The complexes chosen in Step 3 compute $X\times_Y^h Z$ as $X\times_Y\prod_wZ_w=X_E\times_E\prod_wZ_w$ by the Kan model node's homotopy-pullback convention. Its projection to $X_E$ is a trivial Kan fibration, since every boundary lifting problem is the pullback of one for $p$. Therefore the projection to $X$ induces a bijection onto $\pi_0X_E\subseteq\pi_0X$. This proves injectivity without inferring it from connected ordinary fibers. By definition $X_E$ consists exactly of those components whose restrictions send each $w$ to an invertible class in $\pi_0(RT)$. The framed mapping node identifies these components with homotopy classes and identifies their induced functors on path-component categories. Since $\pi_0T\to\pi_0(RT)$ is an equivalence, this says exactly that the induced functor $\pi_0C\to\pi_0T$ sends every $w\in W$ to an isomorphism, independent of natural-isomorphism choices. In particular the identity class of $L_WC$ shows that $q$ inverts $W$.

source.place: Appendix A.3.5, Proposition A.3.5.5; agent proof by pullback of a trivial Kan fibration, using the full function-complex criterion rather than only pi_0.

proof.text: If $(L,q)$ and $(L\prime,q\prime)$ both satisfy this mapping property, apply it with targets $L\prime$ and $L$. The identity class on $L\prime$ restricted along $q\prime$ and the class induced by $q$ give maps under $C$ in both directions. Applying injectivity to the two composites, whose restrictions to $C$ are identities, shows that the composites are identities in $h\mathrm{sCat}$. Thus the two pairs are isomorphic under $C$; the same restriction argument proves uniqueness of the isomorphism.

For an enriched functor carrying each specified arrow of $C$ into the specified arrow set of $C\prime$, the naturality clause of the derived-pushout mapping node supplies the induced map between the two derived pushouts in $h\mathrm{sCat}$. Restriction of mapping classes commutes with this map. Applying the uniqueness argument to identity and composite maps shows that the construction is independent of replacement choices and preserves composition and identities.

lean.statement: theorem simplicial_inversion_universal_property : ∃ B : BergnerModelData.{u}, B.model.categoryWithWeakEquivalences.weakEquivalences = SSet.Bergner.dwyerKanEquivalences ∧ B.model.categoryWithCofibrations.cofibrations = SSet.Bergner.I.rlp.llp ∧ (∀ R : SSet.Bergner.IntervalRepresentatives.{u}, B.model.categoryWithFibrations.fibrations = (SSet.Bergner.J R).rlp) ∧ (∀ P : Pair.{u}, ∃ (L : SCat.{u}) (q : P.category ⟶ L), Nonempty (LocalizationPresentation B P q)) ∧ (∀ (P : Pair.{u}) (L : SCat.{u}) (q : P.category ⟶ L), Nonempty (LocalizationPresentation B P q) → MappingProperty P (bergnerHomotopyFunctor.map q) ∧ Uniqueness P (bergnerHomotopyFunctor.map q)) ∧ InducedMaps.{u} ∧ CompositionCompatibility.{u}
lean.note: Uses the existing marked pairs, resolved derived-pushout presentation and Bergner homotopy category; the downstream comparison theorem is not used. Inversion is tested on a three-arrow representative whose source map is I-injective, ensuring that every original marked vertex lifts. No arbitrary strict inverse choices, saturation hypothesis or local Kan assumption on C or T.
